intro: “Ever” (at any time in your life) and “never” (at no time) are very often used with the present perfect to talk about experiences: “Have you ever been to Canada?”, “I've never eaten snails”. They are the key words for talking about what you have done in your life.
objectifs: Ask about experiences with “Have you ever + past participle?”.
Answer with never, without a double negative.
Put ever and never in the right place in the sentence.
Use “the first time”, “before” and “superlative + I've ever” to give richer answers.

sections.titre: Have you ever…?: the experience question
texte: “Ever” means “at any time in your life until now”. Put it between have / has and the past participle: Have you ever + past participle?
Do not use “already” for this kind of question. “Already” has a different meaning (lesson 53). For life experience, use “ever”.
exemples: Have you ever been to Canada?
At any time in your life.
Has she ever worked abroad?
has + she + ever + participle.
Have your parents ever seen snow?
A question about experience.

texte: Answer with a short answer (Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.), or with “No, never.” If the answer is yes, we often add details in the past simple (lesson 51).
In a full negative answer, “never” replaces “not”: I've never + past participle. Never use never and not together (no double negative).

lignes: Yes, I have. I ate it in Douala last year.
Has he ever ridden a horse?
No, he's never ridden a horse.
Have they ever met your boss?

texte: “Never” goes between have / has and the past participle: “I have never seen”, “She's never been”. It is already negative, so the verb stays positive.
“I haven't ever…” exists, but it is much less common; prefer “I've never…”. To stress that an experience is new, add “before” at the end: “I've never done this before”.
exemples: I've never been to Belgium.
never = not at any time.
My grandmother has never used a computer.
has + never + participle.
We've never tried Ethiopian food before.
before at the end = until now.

sections.titre: Ever with a superlative and “the first time”
texte: “Superlative + noun + I've ever + past participle” describes an exceptional experience: “the best … I've ever …”.
“It's the first time + I've + past participle” says something is happening for the first time. English uses the present perfect here, not the present simple.
exemples: It's the most beautiful place I've ever seen.
Superlative + I've ever.
This is the best coffee I've ever had.
the best … I've ever …
It's the first time I've flown.
Not “the first time I fly”.

sections.titre: Ever and never with other tenses
texte: “Never” is also used with the present simple for habits (I never drink coffee, lesson 7) and with the past simple for a finished period: “My father never learned to swim” (the period of his life we are talking about is over).
In American English, people often say “Did you ever…?” where British English says “Have you ever…?”. For now, use “Have you ever…?” for life experience.
exemples: I never eat meat on Fridays.
Habit: present simple.
I never met my grandfather. He died before I was born.
Finished period: past simple.

formule: Have / Has + subject + ever + past participle? · subject + have / has + never + past participle
prononciation: “ever” is /ˈevə/ (UK) / /ˈevər/ (US); “never” is /ˈnevə/: a short e as in “pet”.
In “Have you ever…?”, the words link: /həv juː ˈevə/; “you ever” sounds almost like /juˈwevə/.
In negative sentences, stress “never”: I've NEVER been there.
“Have you ever…?” goes up at the end (yes / no question); the answer “No, never” goes down.
erreurs: Did you ever go to Paris?
Have you ever been to Paris?
For life experience (standard British English): present perfect.
I haven't never seen it.
I've never seen it.
No double negative: never is enough.
I've ever been to London.
I've been to London.
ever is not used in a simple positive sentence.
Have you already been to Canada?
Have you ever been to Canada?
Life experience: ever, not already.
I never have seen snow.
I've never seen snow.
never goes between have and the participle.
It's the first time I see the sea.
It's the first time I've seen the sea.
After “the first time”: present perfect.
Have you ever went to Lomé?
Have you ever been to Lomé?
After have: past participle (been / gone), not the past simple.

dialogue.contexte: During a lunch break in Montreal, some colleagues play “Have you ever…?”.
lignes: OK, my turn. Have you ever eaten poutine, Kwame?
Yes, I have! I had it on my first day here. It's the best snack I've ever eaten.
Detail in the past simple; superlative + I've ever.
Ha! And have you ever been skiing?
No, never. I've never even seen a ski slope!
Yes, lots of times. I went to Mont-Tremblant last winter.
Can you teach me? It'll be the first time I've tried a winter sport!
Great idea. Let's all go next Saturday!

mots: Have you ever met a famous person?
at an earlier time; until now
to test something to see if you like it
soft white frozen water that falls from the sky
to travel on a bike, motorbike or horse (ride – rode – ridden)
It's the first time I've cooked for ten people.

items: Have you ___ been to Ghana?
ever
I've ___ eaten frogs' legs.
never
Has your brother ___ worked in a restaurant?
ever
She's ___ flown in a plane. She's a bit nervous.
never
It's the best film I've ___ seen.
ever

exercices.consigne: Write the question with Have / Has … ever …?
items: you / climb / a mountain
Have you ever climbed a mountain?
she / lose / her passport
Has she ever lost her passport?
they / see / a lion
Have they ever seen a lion?
he / write / a poem
Has he ever written a poem?

exercices.consigne: Answer the question (✓ = yes, with a detail in the past simple; ✗ = no, with never).
items: Have you ever been to Brussels? (✓ last year)
Yes, I have. I went there last year.
Have you ever played golf? (✗)
No, I've never played golf.
Has Ana ever driven a truck? (✗)
No, she's never driven a truck.
Have you ever met a celebrity? (✓ in 2020)
Yes, I have. I met one in 2020.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I haven't never been to Spain.
I've never been to Spain.
Have you ever saw a ghost?
Have you ever seen a ghost?
It's the first time I eat cassava.
It's the first time I've eaten cassava.
I've ever visited Rome.
I've visited Rome.

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with the word or pattern in brackets.
items: Is snow something you have seen in your life? (ever)
Have you ever seen snow?
We haven't been to South Africa at any time. (never)
We've never been to South Africa.
I have received many presents. This one is the best. (the best … ever)
It's the best present I've ever received.

exercices.consigne: Write three “Have you ever…?” questions for a friend, then answer them for yourself (yes with a detail in the past simple, or no with never).
items: Model answer

Have you ever slept in a tent? — Yes, I have. I slept in a tent near Kribi in 2019. Have you ever run a marathon? — No, I've never run a marathon. Have you ever cooked for a big party? — Yes, I have. I cooked for my sister's wedding last year.

a_retenir: Have you ever + past participle? = life experience (ever = at any time in your life).
I've never + past participle: never is already negative, no not.
ever and never go between have / has and the participle.
If yes, give the details (when, where) in the past simple.
the best … I've ever …; It's the first time I've + past participle.
